1:1.t: "Silas": the KJV's "Silvanus", the Latin form of his name (Acts 15:22). Paul founded the church at Thessalonica on his second journey (Acts 17:1-10); this is probably one of his earliest letters, about AD 50.
"From God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words.

2:7.t: "Gentle": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "little children" (one letter differs in Greek).

2:14.t: Paul speaks of those Jews in Judea who opposed the gospel, not of the Jewish people as a whole; he was himself a Jew, as were Jesus and the first believers. Compare Romans 9:1-5 and 11:1-2.

3:2.t: "God's servant": the KJV's "minister of God"; some manuscripts read "God's co-worker".

4:4.t: "Control your own body": the KJV's "possess his vessel". "Vessel" may mean one's own body or one's wife (compare 1 Peter 3:7).

4:15.t: "Precede": the KJV's "prevent", which in 1611 meant "go before".
"Coming" (Greek parousia): arrival or presence, used of a king's official visit; it became the term for Christ's return. See Matthew 24:3.

5:22.t: "Every form of evil": the KJV's "all appearance of evil". The Greek eidos means "kind" or "form", not outward appearance.

4:13.t: "Sleep" (Greek koimao): the New Testament often speaks of believers' death as sleep, because they will be raised; see Acts 7:60. Christians grieve, but not as those without hope.

4:17.t: "Caught up" (Greek harpagesometha, Latin rapiemur): the source of the word "rapture". "To meet" (Greek apantesis): used of a city's delegation going out to meet an arriving king and escort him back. Christians differ on the order of end-time events; Paul's purpose here is comfort: all believers, living and dead, will be with the Lord.

5:2.t: "The day of the Lord": the Old Testament day of God's judgment and salvation (Amos 5:18, Joel 2:31), now linked to Christ's return.

5:23.t: "Spirit, soul and body": Paul's way of saying "the whole person", not necessarily a precise three-part division.
